newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish military acts in dispute with Islamists.
newsitem.headline: Turkish military acts in dispute with Islamists.

text.p: A marathon meeting of Turkey's secularist army ended on Monday with an announcement that it had taken "necessary decisions" to deal with suspected Moslem activists in its ranks.
A television station said the generals had imposed their will on Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan and dismissed officers suspected of Islamist tendencies.
"The discipline and moral position of some members of the Turkish armed forces was evaluated and the necessary decisions were taken," the Supreme Military Council said in a short statement.
Military officials declined to comment on the statement, which gave no details of the decisions taken.
The NTV television news channel said Erbakan had bowed to military demands at the army meeting to approve the discharge of an undisclosed number of suspected pro-Islamist officers.
"Prime Minister Erbakan objected to some of the expulsion dossiers but signed the vast majority of them," NTV said.
Newspapers had said earlier that about 100 officers and non-commissioned officers, most of them accused of being Islamists, were to be drummed out of the army.

Monday's meeting had been watched by the political establishment and financial markets for any effect it could have on the future of Erbakan's Islamist-led coalition, brought to breaking point by previous army pressure for an end to an Islamist resurgence.
Istanbul stock exchange closed before the six-hour meeting had finished. Shares ended 0.2 percent up.
Anatolian news agency said the main opposition Motherland Party was considering a fresh censure motion in parliament against the ruling alliance.
"The schedule of the censure motion, if it is brought, will be completed by June 10," the agency said.
Erbakan last week narrowly survived a censure motion in parliament with the support of six MPs from a far-right party.
Four deputies from the conservative True Path Party wing of the coalition have since resigned, reducing the government's majority to one in the 550-seat parliament.
Erbakan attracted the wrath of NATO member Turkey's secularist elite in February when he announced a series of mild Islamist prosposals.
True Path leader Tansu Ciller, also the foreign minister, held one-to-one meetings with a dozen MPs on Monday in an apparent attempt to stall a backbencher rebellion against the the government.
The security apparatus has so far been the Islamists' most determined opponent.
A prosecutor last week filed a case at the constitutional court for the banning of Welfare for its alleged undermining of Turkey's secularist principles.
A Moslem preacher close to Welfare appeared in a security court charged with urging the establishment of sharia Islamic law in a Friday prayers sermon, Anatolian news agency said.
Police also arrested 17 people in the southern coastal city of Antalya for membership of an illegal Islamic group and trying to overthrow the constitutional regime, the agency said.

Erbakan, modern Turkey's first Islamist leader, congratulated Iran's president-elect Mohammad Khatami on his election victory and called for good relations despite a diplomatic row over a Turkish army incursion into northern Iraq.
Iran has protested to Turkey over its cross-border offensive against Kurdistan Workers Party rebels in northern Iraq.
